why: Concrete, builds toward an action (map your bet), shorter and more practical than reciting Cagan's four risks.
Cuts the narrator backstory and the anxiety/insufficiency declaration; fewer sentences, keeps the core first-person line.
The guess prompt sits after the setup and before the second session runs, so the student actually guesses before seeing the answer.
Puts the student in control by shaping the rules together; A's 'You are not drafting from a blank page' is a flat restatement.
Fewer words, and B's added sentence is vague and dull about what to do.
'One run at a time' is a more precise, picturable unit than 'session', and the closing sentence is unchanged otherwise.
The title carries the concept and the closer 'Taste closes the gap' stays short and not repeated; B restates the title as a closer.
B adds a clutter reference to M6 and a closer 'flywheel' line, an unbuilt metaphor; A is shorter.
Cuts the extra clause 'the shape the whole map has had from the start', which is wordy abstraction.
B's closing sentence is an extra moralising closer; cut it.
'Exercise' is the right word for what was run; 'prompts' is the wrong unit and A is the clearer reference.
Shorter and tighter, and 'this scrollback' is simpler than 'this session's scrollback'; the extra clause is redundant.
B's forward hint to Module 4 is a closer and an abstract pointer; A is shorter and states the practice.
'YOUR real work is the material' is neutral and drops the shouted 'runs on'; roughly equal, B slightly cleaner.
B's added 'The move is the same every time' is a restating filler sentence; A is shorter.
B adds a forward hint about Phases 3 and 4; cut forward hints.
B cuts the narrated loop-steps sentence; fewer words, same point.
'It often isn't. It's a draft' is more accurate than the always-true-only-sometimes 'often just a draft'; matches the author's no-untrue-claims rule.
A's added sentence says what students are not learning, a put-down-ish hedge and extra words; B is shorter.
B tells the room what to do (watch rather than type along), a trainer-to-room pace frame, though A is plainer; B gives clear guidance on pace.
'three' is wrong or at least counts oddly (the list has Verification, Absorption, Outcome, fine) but A avoids the numeral and a made-up count; neutral and shorter.
Title says 'Three pressures' and lists exactly three; B's vague 'Pressures' loses information.
'Three agents using the file' is a concrete, pictureable title; 'Where the file gets read' is more abstract.
B is shorter and simpler; 'what it leaves out' is a concrete question to ask the agent.
B adds a closer that restates and tells the student what their practice is; cut it.
B piles on count-after-count in a list; A is more concrete and the 'visible confidence' framing is cleaner, though B's trimmed first half is tighter. Overall A wins by avoiding the extra recital.
B's 'This is your side-quest lane' is an extra sentence adding nothing.
B adds a hedging lead sentence; A is shorter and starts directly on the concept.
'Check' vs 'Read': author wants precise verbs; 'read' implies reading all of it, while 'check' fits the act of judging a proposal.
B's 'forest before the trees' is a loaded flourish metaphor not built in the course; A states the point neutrally.
A's title states the action ('A check resets the chain') and is shorter; B's title is wordier.
A's title is a concrete instruction the student can act on; B's is a statement about the LLM.
Author kept B: it offers the recommended live option (/statusline) rather than the vaguer 'ask Claude to set up'.
B's 'a future engineer can inspect' is wordier and adds an abstract clause; A is plain.
A's made-up concept 'The wall' is the author-rejected invented abstraction; B says it plainly.
A's title is concrete and pictureable; B's title is an abstract claim.
Shorter header, same meaning; 'context' is redundant with the body.
Extra closer is a restatement and a cheap highlight; fewer sentences.
Drops the count from the header, which would break if the list changes; fewer words.
Concise instruction replaces a redundant lead-in sentence; the prompt does the work.
The closing line clarifies how to read the phases and prevents a pipeline misreading.
Permission framing ('don't need to get it right first time') lands the experiment stance again with its why.
Concrete action the student takes, in few words; B is abstract and wordy.
Cuts connective filler sentences; orientation is already clear from the links.
'Alternative' is the plainer word; 'gives you the floor' and 'committed change' are abstract and wordier.
